subtopics.title: PSLV-C62 failure and its cause
subtopics.summary: ISRO's first launch of 2026, PSLV-C62, was scheduled from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh. A third-stage solid rocket anomaly disrupted high-thrust delivery to the upper stages, which affected the intended satellite orbital injection. The failure came 8 months after the PSLV-C61 setback.

Fault: 3rd-stage solid rocket anomaly

Impact: intended satellite orbital injection affected
Failure came 8 months after the PSLV-C61 setback

subtopics.title: PSLV rocket profile and history
subtopics.summary: The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle is called the Workhorse of ISRO and is a four-stage medium-lift launcher, first launched in 1993. It uses solid propellants in its first and third stages and liquid propellants in its second (Vikas engine) and fourth stages. It can carry up to 1750 kg to a 600 km Sun-synchronous orbit.
facts: Nickname: Workhorse of ISRO

Launched in 1993; first success in 1994 with IRS-P2
Stages 1 and 3 use solid propellants
Stages 2 (Vikas engine) and 4 use liquid propellants
First Indian launch vehicle equipped with liquid stages
Payload: up to 1750 kg to a 600 km Sun-synchronous orbit
Record: 104 satellites in one launch (2017)
Notable missions: Chandrayaan-1, Mars Orbiter Mission, Aditya-L1, AstroSat

subtopics.title: PSLV-C62 payloads
subtopics.summary: PSLV-C62 carried EOS-N1 (Anvesha), a hyperspectral imaging satellite developed for DRDO's Strategic Applications, and KID, a small re-entry prototype from a Spanish startup. It also carried AayulSAT, India's first on-orbit satellite refuelling payload. In total, 18 co-passenger satellites flew on the mission.

subtopics.title: ISRO launch vehicles, private players and policy
subtopics.summary: India's launch vehicle family ranges from the early SLV and GSLV to the planned NGLV, which has a maximum payload capability of 30 tonnes. The SSLV serves small satellites and takes that load off the PSLV. Private firms such as Agnikul Cosmos are building their own rockets, which the Indian Space Policy 2023 allows.

quizzes.title: PSLV-C62 mission check
quizzes.passage:
ISRO planned its first launch of 2026 with PSLV-C62, a rocket scheduled to lift off from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh. The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle is often called the workhorse of ISRO, and this flight carried a mix of government and commercial satellites. During the mission, a fault appeared in the third stage. A solid rocket anomaly disrupted the high-thrust delivery to the upper stages, and this affected the planned injection of the satellites into orbit. The failure came after an earlier setback with PSLV-C61, which put the vehicle under close scrutiny.

Among the payloads was EOS-N1, also known as Anvesha, an Earth observation satellite built for strategic applications. Another payload was KID, a small re-entry prototype developed by a Spanish startup, which was meant to splash down in the ocean. The flight also carried AayulSAT, a satellite refuelling payload from a Bengaluru company, and a group of co-passenger satellites from several countries. Together, the payloads covered Earth observation, re-entry testing and satellite refuelling. Each payload was carried on the same rocket, so a fault in the upper stages put all of them at risk. The rocket's earlier flights, including missions to the Moon and Mars, show why its reliability matters for the national programme.

quizzes.title: PSLV profile recall
quizzes.passage: The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle is widely known as the workhorse of the Indian Space Research Organisation. It is a medium-lift launcher with four stages, and it has carried many national missions, including lunar and Mars missions. Its design mixes two kinds of propulsion, since some stages burn solid fuel while others use liquid propellants. Because of this mix, it became the first Indian launch vehicle to be equipped with liquid stages, a milestone for the national programme. The rocket also holds a notable record of its own, having carried a very large number of satellites on a single flight. It is able to place heavy satellites into a Sun-synchronous orbit, which suits Earth observation work. Over the years it has launched satellites for both government and commercial customers, reflecting its reliability and flexibility. The rocket's stages fire one after another, and the upper stages must deliver steady thrust for satellites to reach their planned orbit. This makes the vehicle an important tool for both national missions and international customers. Its success has made it a central part of India's launch plans, and it continues to be a core vehicle in the country's space efforts.
